newsitem.title: CANADA: Chretien campaign hit by disturbance, jobless rate.
newsitem.headline: Chretien campaign hit by disturbance, jobless rate.

text.p: Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien was forced to cancel a campaign event on Friday by an angry crowd complaining of unemployment and the plight of fishermen.
The prime minister was never threatened by the crowd, but about 300 protesters shouting "We want jobs" blocked a media bus that was planning to cover the event.
The demonstrators rocked the bus, broke its windshield wipers and prevented it from moving onto the site of the massive Hibernia oil project that Chretien was to have toured.

Liberal Party campaign plans were thrown into disarray and Chretien's entourage, which had been scheduled to arrive about 45 minutes after the journalists, eventually turned back along with the media bus to the Newfoundland capital of St. John's, 90 miles (140 km) to the east.

"Frankly this isn't how we discuss policy differences in Canada. It's a rather unfortunate incident. It's still unclear whether or not we'll be able to go ahead with the visit to Hibernia," Chretien spokesman Sean Kirby said from Ottawa.

It was not clear whether he might fly in by helicopter in the afternoon. He was to have inaugurated a new oil platform as part of the C$5.8 billion ($4.2 billion U.S.) Hibernia oil project, scheduled to start producing in late 1997.
It has been one of the economic hopes for Newfoundland, Canada's poorest province where fishermen face depleted stocks and unemployment runs at 19.1 percent.
Buzz Hargrove, president of the Canadian Auto Workers union, was among the crowd, which carried signs decrying the Liberal federal government's tough fishing policies: "Empty nets, empty promises."

For the Liberals, the labor disturbance could not have come on a worse day -- the same morning as the federal agency Statistics Canada revealed that the country's unemployment rate climbed to 9.6 percent in April from 9.3 percent.
The widely awaited figure will be the last such release before the June 2 election that Chretien called, 1-1/2 years before he was required to, in order to cash in on a lead in the polls.
Chretien spokesman Patrick Parisot, who was stranded with reporters at the back of the media bus, pointed to the fact that 33,000 new jobs had been created.
Nonetheless, the jobless rate was still between nine and 10 percent for most of Chretien's mandate.

Chretien's chief economic legacy has been to wrestle Canada's chronic budget deficits to the ground, thus helping interest rates plummet. In cutting spending, he has won the disapproval of big labor and the leftist New Democratic Party.
He has also faced a stiff challenge on the right from the Reform Party and the Conservative Party, which have been pressing for tax cuts, especially on payrolls.

"The unemployment numbers aren't going to get better until the government removes the biggest obstacle to job creation in our country, namely high taxes," Reform campaign director Rick Anderson said by phone.

Conservative spokesman Tom Van Dusen slammed the Liberal spin on the numbers: "It's a smokescreen. The issue is the jobless rate. (There are) still 1-1/2 million (jobless) Canadians. That's the number that has to be tackled head on."
